summary: Defines a new mail header, Message-Context, based on RFC 2822, that gives information about the context and presentation of a message. A receiving mail client may use it as a hint for how best to present the message, for example as voice mail or fax.

eli5.summary: This is a small label on an email that says what kind of message it is, so the mail program can show it in a fitting way.

questions: how does a mail client use message-context
subtitle: A mail header that hints whether a message is voice mail, a fax, a page or ordinary email.

tldr.problem: A mail client often cannot tell whether a message is voice mail, a fax, a page or plain email, because the media types inside do not reveal the sender's intent.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a top-level Message-Context header whose value is an IANA-registered class such as voice-message or fax-message, which the receiving user agent may use as a presentation hint.
tldr.outcome: It is only a hint: a receiver must still show a message correctly if the value is wrong. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3938.

today: RFC 3458 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2003 and has been updated by RFC 3938.

sections.title: A Header for Message Context
sections.content:
RFC 3458 defines a mechanism that lets the sender of an Internet mail message convey its contextual information. The message context describes the way the user expects to interact with the message: for example e-mail, voice mail or fax mail. A receiving user agent (UA) can use it to improve presentation.

The mechanism is an RFC 2822 header called Message-Context. It is in some ways similar to the Content-Disposition MIME entity, which gives clues for how to display a body part; Message-Context gives clues for the message as a whole.

The RFC lists typical uses: selecting a special viewer for a message, selecting an icon in a message list, arranging messages in an inbox display, and filtering messages when the user has limited access.
sections.eli5: A mail program usually treats every message the same. This label lets the sender say what sort of message it is, so the program can show a fitting icon or viewer.

sections.title: Why Media Types Are Not Enough
sections.content:
Multimedia messaging systems receive messages that a UA may present in many ways. One UA may print fax images automatically, another may play voice messages through a telephone handset. A common request is a "universal inbox" that lists everything together, and in "unified messaging" some users treat voice mail as implicitly urgent and want to find it quickly.

Deciding the context is hard from content alone. A message with audio and image data could be a fax with voice commentary, a voice message with diagrams, or a true multimedia message. A message with text and audio could be e-mail with an MP3 attached, or a voice message with a text header for non-voice readers.

The RFC states that message context relates to media content but is not the same thing. Text e-mail and an SMS message share a media type yet have different user contexts.
sections.eli5: If you find a picture and a recording in an envelope, you cannot tell whether it is a fax with a voice note or a voice message with a picture. The sender's label settles it.

sections.title: Why a New Top-Level Header
sections.content:
Inspecting the media types would force the UA to scan the whole message, which is burdensome for large voice and video objects. The authors also considered registering a multipart/* subtype, as the VPIM Work Group did with multipart/voice-message. That type is syntactically identical to multipart/mixed, and Content-Type refers to a body part, not to the whole message.

Creating aliases for multipart/mixed would also remove the option of marking a message as multipart/alternate, multipart/parallel or multipart/encrypted. Since the context is an attribute of the entire message, the RFC defines a new top-level message attribute instead.

Message-Context only identifies the context. It does not say what content the UA must be able to deliver, and it implies no disposition or delivery notification. The functional requirements add that wrong or invalid classification must not cause a transfer failure or prevent presentation, and that the mechanism should be extensible to new kinds of messages.
sections.eli5: Opening a whole big package just to see what is in it would be slow. A label on the outside lets you decide without opening it.

sections.title: The Message-Context Field and Its Classes
sections.content:
The sending UA inserts the field as a top-level header. Its form is Message-Context: message-context-class, and both the field name and the class values are not case sensitive. The class is an IANA-registered value.

The initial classes are voice-message (a voice mail message), fax-message (a facsimile mail message), pager-message (a page, such as a text or numeric pager message or an SMS message), multimedia-message (an aggregate multimedia message, such as an MHTML message), text-message (a traditional Internet mail message) and none (no context information).

The registration states the header may appear a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 1 times in a message.
sections.eli5: The sticker has only a few words to pick from: voice, fax, pager, multimedia, text, or none for no sticker at all.

sections.title: How Receivers Must Treat It
sections.content:
A receiving UA MUST NOT depend on the indicated value in a way that prevents proper presentation. If the value is wrong or does not match the content, the UA MUST still display the message at least as meaningfully as it would with no Message-Context at all. If the header is missing, the UA MUST treat the message as if the value were none.

The UA may use the context to decide whether, when and possibly where to display a message, but it should not alter the actual rendering. A voice-message should not be sent to a fax terminal, yet a voice-message that arrives with only fax content at a multimedia terminal with a printer must still be rendered properly. A voice message that has had its audio stripped by a gateway, leaving only a text part, is still in the voice message context.

The RFC does not specify UA behavior when forwarding a message, beyond noting that a context-aware UA should provide a meaningful value.
sections.eli5: The sticker is only a hint. If it is wrong, the mail program must still show the message properly and not throw an error.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The header is meant to be an indicator of context only. The RFC warns that someone could create an "Application" context, and a poorly designed UA could blindly execute a mailed program based on it. Its advice is not to do that.

An attacker could also bomb a receiver with messages whose Message-Context does not fit their body parts, a form of denial of service. That is why the receiver treats the value as a hint only.
sections.eli5: A sticker can lie. A mail program must never run something just because a sticker says to, and should not be fooled by wrong stickers.

sections.title: The IANA Registry of Context Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers Message-Context as a new top-level RFC 2822 message header. It also has IANA create a repository called "Internet Message Context Types" with a "Specification Required" policy by RFC. Section 8.1 of the RFC lists the initial values.

To add a new message context type, you MUST publish an RFC documenting it, include the registration template in its IANA Considerations section, and describe any interoperability and security issues. The template asks for a class name, a summary of no more than 4 lines, and a contact person and email address.
sections.eli5: New sticker types are not made up on the spot. They go in an official list, and a new one needs its own published document first.

items.label: Voice mail
items.desc: Primary content is audio data, usually recorded from a voice telephone call.

items.label: Fax mail
items.desc: Primary content is image data, usually from a facsimile telephone call.

items.label: Page
items.desc: Primary content is text, an urgent message usually of limited length.

items.label: Multimedia
items.desc: Aggregate multimedia message, most likely MHTML.

items.label: Classic email
items.desc: Traditional text-based Internet message, with or without attachments.

items.label: No context
items.desc: No context information; also the default when the header is absent.
